# Introduction and Orientation

This is an online course book, designed for students on the Warwick Business School MRes Programme, who are taking the module 'Learning from Data (and) Science'. The module consists of a set of in-person lectures, linked with these examples and additional expositions.

You can see to the left a list of the contents of the book. However, please note that these 'chapter numbers' do not refer to the specific lectures. Not all of the lectures use quantitative examples.

It is important to note that this module is not designed to teach you how to use R. The objective of the module is to help you learn how to use and interpret the results of quantitative social science research, understand the core principles of excellent quantitative social science, and also how to apply key principles of quantitative and scientific thinking into your own life and (where relevant) work.

This book is written in **Markdown**, using R and the **bookdown** package, and published online in HTML format. A full archive of all the R Code and data for the individual chapters from the book is available from Professor Lee on request, once the book is completed for the year.

This book is essentially a 'live' document, meaning that it is finalised for each year just before the module runs, but then modified for future runnings.

The current year is `r format(Sys.Date(), "%Y")`, and the book is currently *in progress for `r format(Sys.Date(), "%Y")`.*

## How this book works {#how-this-book-works}

Most chapters follow the same basic pattern. Each one takes a core idea, such as what a correlation really tells you, why a p-value is so easily misread, or how a relationship can be manufactured out of nothing, and teaches it through the simplest method that will do the job. Often that means a simulation: rather than asking you to take a claim on trust, I build a small world where we know the truth and show you what the method does in it. The R code is there for you to run and change. You'll learn far more by breaking it than by reading it.

Simple methods are deliberate. Most of you will spend far more of your careers *reading* quantitative research than doing it, and the papers you read will use methods much more complicated than anything in this book. The good news is that those methods rest on the same handful of core ideas. So several chapters end with a section called **Reading the literature**, and more will be added as the book develops. These sections take the chapter's core idea and show you where it turns up in published research, including in methods the book doesn't teach you to run, so that when you meet an odds ratio, a control function or a pre-registration in a paper, you'll know what it's claiming and what to ask about it. Each one ends with a few suggestions for further reading, chosen for people who want to understand the ideas rather than become specialists.

Finally, each chapter lists the references it cites at its end, so you can follow up anything that interests you.

Please enjoy the book, and learn from it.

Feel free to email me with any questions or comments: nick.lee@wbs.ac.uk
